name: Backfill capability
summary: The ability to populate or repair historical data after the fact — a new column, corrected logic, or late-arriving records.
description: Backfill capability is how easily a system can go back and fill in or fix history: adding a column across all past partitions, re-deriving a metric after a logic change, or absorbing late-arriving data into the right time buckets. It is strongest where a target can be reprocessed by partition or date range from retained raw, and where models support a full-refresh or MERGE without disrupting live reads. It is limited in pure-streaming designs that lack a bounded batch path, and constrained wherever history was not retained or the target cannot be selectively rewritten.

mechanisms.name: Partitioned reprocessing
mechanisms.note: Rewriting only the affected date/key partitions lets a backfill target a bounded slice of history without recomputing the entire table.

mechanisms.name: Incremental models with full-refresh
mechanisms.note: Transformation frameworks expose a full-refresh switch to rebuild an incremental model end-to-end after logic changes, then resume incremental runs.

mechanisms.name: Parameterized date-range runs
mechanisms.note: Orchestrated jobs accept start/end parameters so a backfill can be scheduled across historical windows, often as fan-out per-partition tasks.

mechanisms.name: MERGE / upsert into target
mechanisms.note: Backfilled rows are merged on key so re-filling a window updates or inserts without duplicating existing records or disturbing untouched partitions.

mechanisms.name: Immutable raw retention
mechanisms.note: Keeping source data append-only means the inputs needed to reconstruct any past period are always available to feed a backfill.

manifestations.statement: Immutable bronze retains all raw history and silver/gold rebuild by partition, so adding a column or fixing logic is a routine partitioned reprocess merged into the affected windows.
Staging preserves source data and dbt incremental models support full-refresh, so backfilling a new column or corrected metric across history is a first-class, well-tooled operation.
Raw is loaded warehouse-native and dbt full-refresh plus parameterized runs make date-range backfills straightforward, bounded mainly by warehouse compute cost, not by capability.
Partition-level rewrites and MERGE let a backfill surgically replace or fill specific historical partitions while snapshot isolation keeps live readers on a consistent version throughout.
Continuous commits still land in a partitioned table format, so a bounded batch job can backfill or correct historical partitions alongside the live stream without stopping it.
The batch layer exists specifically to recompute authoritative history from master data, making backfills of corrected logic or late data a designed-for responsibility of the architecture.
Parameterized date-range reruns can backfill a target, but success depends on retained raw extracts and idempotent loads; overwritten sources cap how far a backfill can reach.
Facts can be reloaded by partition and dimensions re-keyed, but backfilling a new attribute across historical Type-2 rows is fiddly and may require reconstructing surrogate-key lineage.
Insert-only satellites make it clean to add new attributes going forward and recompute marts, but truly backfilling values into past effective-dated records requires careful new satellite loads.

A one-time snapshot re-seed can backfill the mirror, but because CDC tracks only current state, backfilling historical as-of values requires an external archive of change events the mirror doesn't keep.
Late-arriving device data is absorbed by re-aggregating affected time windows from retained raw, though very high volume and short hot-tier retention can limit how far back a backfill is practical.
Offline features backfill by recomputing point-in-time-correct values over history, but keeping the online store consistent with a backfilled offline store adds real operational complexity.
Immutable raw retention means the inputs for any backfill are available, but with no managed target the backfill itself is bespoke per consumer rather than a standard partitioned rewrite.
With no batch path, backfilling a new column or late correction means replaying the whole log through a reprocessing job — feasible but heavyweight, and awkward for targeted historical fixes.
Serving stores are tuned for fresh low-latency reads with short retention, so correcting deep history usually means a full rebuild from an upstream source rather than an in-place backfill.
Backfilling means re-emitting or replaying historical events, but downstream consumers may not tolerate old events arriving late, so retroactive corrections are constrained by consumer contracts.
Backfilling into SaaS destinations re-pushes history into live business tools, which is often unsafe or rate-limited; the destination, not the pipeline, dictates whether a backfill is even permitted.
Federation materializes nothing of its own, so there is no target to backfill; any historical correction must happen in the underlying source systems it merely queries.

tradeoffs.title: Cost efficiency
tradeoffs.note: Backfilling means recomputing large historical ranges and retaining immutable raw history to recompute from, both of which consume substantial extra compute and storage.

tradeoffs.title: Throughput
tradeoffs.note: A large backfill contends with live loads for cluster and warehouse resources, degrading the effective throughput of current pipelines while it runs.

tradeoffs.title: Maintainability
tradeoffs.note: Pipelines must be idempotent and fully parameterized by date range so any window can be re-run safely, forcing disciplined partition and re-run design across every job.
